content: The ratio of dogs to humans varies significantly across different regions, and inaccuracies in human census data can compromise the precision of dog population estimates. Additionally, underreporting and inconsistent patterns of dog ownership in urban areas further complicate accurate assessments of dog populations. Alternative methods for estimating dog populations include surveys and capture-mark-recapture techniques, which are particularly effective for free-roaming dogs. These methods are detailed in the Canine Rabies Blueprint and are often combined with post-vaccination surveys to evaluate vaccination coverage and refine population estimates for future campaigns. Data from dog registries can be helpful but are inherently limited as they exclude unregistered or stray dogs, leading to underestimation of the total dog population. Low or uneven vaccination coverage, even if the regional average is high, can allow rabies to persist and hinder elimination efforts. Vaccination campaigns are most effective when conducted systematically across contiguous areas with comprehensive coverage, rather than in fragmented, isolated regions. Proactive, annual vaccination campaigns are recommended unless surveillance indicates a significant reduction in rabies incidence in specific areas. Reactive strategies are less effective and take longer to control rabies compared to systematic vaccination efforts. Achieving the required immunization coverage necessitates well-designed educational campaigns, intersectoral and interdisciplinary collaboration, community involvement, local commitment to planning and execution, availability of high-quality vaccines, media support, and effective coordination and supervision by relevant authorities. During mass vaccination campaigns, all dogs, including newborn puppies, should be vaccinated regardless of weight, health status, or prior vaccination history. Herd immunity can be achieved by vaccinating at least 70% of the rabies-susceptible dog population. Puppies, which often constitute a significant portion of the population, are frequently left unvaccinated due to manufacturer or national guidelines, despite evidence from studies in South Africa, Tunisia, and Tanzania showing that young puppies (<3 months old) can mount an effective immune response to high-quality vaccines without adverse effects. Owners and vaccination teams should be informed that vaccinating puppies, including newborns, is essential for adequate population coverage, even if this represents off-label use. Four primary approaches to accessing dogs for vaccination campaigns include house-to-house visits, fixed vaccination posts in well-recognized community sites, temporary posts set up by mobile teams, and mobile street vaccination teams. Vaccination posts are most effective when located within 500 meters or a 10-minute walk from the community. The choice of approach should be tailored to the local sociocultural context, and a combination of methods may be employed. Integrating other health interventions, such as deworming or neutering, into vaccination campaigns can provide additional health benefits and incentivize participation from both dog owners and veterinary practitioners. Vaccination campaigns are typically conducted annually, but more frequent campaigns may be necessary in areas with high rabies incidence, high dog population turnover, or where program goals have not been met. Intensive campaigns lasting less than one month have been effective in controlling rabies in Latin America, Asia, and Africa, provided they achieve at least 70% coverage of the dog population. Campaigns should prioritize coverage over speed and may be scheduled on weekends, during school hours, or holidays to improve turnout, as children often bring their dogs for vaccination. Monitoring vaccination campaigns involves registering and permanently identifying vaccinated dogs, though cost-effective, safe, and simple identification methods that are well-accepted by both dogs and owners are still under research. Temporary identification methods, such as colored tags, paint, spray marks, or plastic collars, have proven useful for identifying vaccinated dogs and motivating owners to participate. Permanent or temporary identification is crucial for evaluating vaccination coverage and distinguishing unvaccinated dogs for follow-up. Routine serological monitoring during mass vaccination campaigns is generally unnecessary if high-quality vaccines are used, vaccination teams are properly trained, and the cold chain is maintained. However, if repeated annual campaigns fail to reduce animal rabies cases, it may indicate non-compliance with these elements or inaccuracies in dog population estimates. Vaccines used in campaigns must be stored within an acceptable temperature range (2–8°C) to maintain efficacy. Vaccines inducing immunity for at least two years should be used in annual campaigns to revaccinate all dogs, as revaccination has no adverse effects. While annual booster vaccinations may not be necessary for dogs receiving long-term immunity vaccines, turning people and their dogs away at vaccination points could send a confusing message. In many campaigns, the direct cost of revaccination is lower than the fixed costs of the campaign. Puppies under three months of age should be included in vaccination campaigns in endemic regions, and vaccination certificates should only be issued after puppies receive a booster dose to account for potential interference from maternal antibodies. Veterinary vaccines for rabies are available as inactivated (killed), modified-live, or recombinant products. Nerve tissue vaccines are less immunogenic and induce more severe adverse reactions than modern cell culture vaccines. WHO and OIE strongly recommend discontinuing nerve tissue vaccines in favor of modern cell culture vaccines. Modified live-virus vaccines for parenteral vaccination of dogs are also discouraged, and inactivated vaccines (with or without adjuvants) are preferred. Vaccination team members handling dogs should receive pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) before campaigns, and adequate post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) should be available for those exposed during campaigns. In cases of accidental exposure to modified live rabies vaccines, medical assistance and PEP should be considered. Oral rabies vaccination (ORV) has been successfully used to control rabies in certain wildlife reservoir species and may improve vaccination coverage in hard-to-reach dog subpopulations. ORV should be conducted by trained vaccinators and is most effective when combined with parenteral vaccination. However, oral vaccines require dogs to be attracted to the bait, chew it, and deposit the vaccine onto the oral mucosa in the correct amount. Parenteral vaccination with inactivated vaccines remains the preferred method for accessible dogs, while ORV can be beneficial for semi-restricted, non-restricted, and unapproachable dog populations. Countries considering ORV should ensure the safety of the viral construct for target and non-target species, including humans, and conduct pilot studies to evaluate feasibility and efficacy before widescale application.
